issues.legal_issue: A second appellate court may not reverse a pure finding of fact without framing a substantial question of law.
material_facts: The first appellate court rejected the alleged earlier sale agreement after considering oral evidence and circumstances bearing on its genuineness.
The High Court reversed that finding in a second appeal without framing a substantial question of law.
Although one factual reason given by the first appellate court was mistaken, its finding rested on other evidence and circumstances.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred by failing to frame a substantial question of law and by interfering with the first appellate court’s pure finding of fact.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires a substantial question of law to be framed before a second appeal is decided. A second appellate court cannot interfere with a finding of fact supported by material. The Court relied on Kshitish Chandra Purkait v. Santosh Kumar Purkait and Sheel Chand v. Prakash Chand.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is a second appeal from a lower appellate court’s decision.
predicates.no_substantial_question_framed: The second appellate court decided the appeal without framing a substantial question of law.
predicates.pure_factual_finding_reversed: The second appellate court reversed a factual finding that was supported by material.

issues.definition: When a second appellate court reverses a supported factual finding without framing a substantial question of law, its interference with that finding is impermissible.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court retains its discretionary power in an appeal after granting special leave and may decline to interfere despite identifying an error in the decision below.
material_facts: The appeal was being heard after special leave had been granted.
The plaintiff knew of the alleged trespass but did not promptly object or seek relief while the two rooms were being constructed.
The plaintiff delayed giving notice and filing suit, and the rooms had remained for many years.
The Court identified errors in the High Court’s treatment of the second appeal but found the circumstances did not warrant disturbing its decree.
issues.conclusion: The Court retained its discretion under Article 136 after granting special leave and declined to interfere with the decree, notwithstanding its determination that the High Court had erred.
issues.legal_principle: The discretionary power under Article 136 continues after special leave is granted. It is exercised sparingly, generally where exceptional circumstances and substantial and grave injustice justify intervention; the Court may declare the law yet decline to interfere or mould relief according to the justice of the case. The Court relied on Pritam Singh v. The State, Hem Raj v. State of Ajmer, M/s Bengal Chemical & Pharmaceutical Works Ltd. v. Their Workmen, and Municipal Board, Pratapgarh v. Mahendra Singh Chawla.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and known_trespass and no_prompt_objection and prolonged_delay and longstanding_structures

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal heard after special leave has been granted.
predicates.known_trespass: The claimant knew that another person had entered onto the disputed land.
predicates.no_prompt_objection: The claimant did not promptly object or seek relief while the construction was underway.
predicates.prolonged_delay: The claimant waited a substantial time before taking formal steps to challenge the occupation.
predicates.longstanding_structures: The structures had remained on the disputed land for many years.

issues.definition: In an appeal heard after special leave, known occupation, failure to object promptly, substantial delay, and long-standing structures may lead the Court to decline interference despite identifying an error.

issues.legal_issue: Where the claimant knew of an encroachment, delayed challenging it while permanent structures were built, and the structures had remained for many years, the Court may substitute payment for the occupied land for possession and removal of the structures.
material_facts: The plaintiff had acquired the disputed land and the defendant occupied it and constructed two rooms.
The plaintiff knew of the occupation but did not promptly object or seek an injunction while construction proceeded.
The plaintiff waited years before giving notice and filing suit.
The rooms had remained for about thirty years by the time of the appeal.
The parties did not agree on the land’s value.
issues.conclusion: The Court left in place the decree dismissing the suit for possession, but modified it to require the defendant to pay the value of the occupied land, with the trial court to determine that value on evidence.
issues.legal_principle: In exercising its discretionary jurisdiction under Article 136, the Court may mould relief to meet the justice of the case and compensate a claimant instead of granting possession and demolition where the circumstances make those remedies inappropriate. The Court relied on the discretionary and relief-moulding principles discussed in Pritam Singh v. The State, Hem Raj v. State of Ajmer, M/s Bengal Chemical & Pharmaceutical Works Ltd. v. Their Workmen, and Municipal Board, Pratapgarh v. Mahendra Singh Chawla.

rule.if: special_leave_civil_appeal and claimant_owned_occupied_land and known_trespass and no_prompt_objection and longstanding_structures

predicates.special_leave_civil_appeal: The proceeding is a civil appeal heard after special leave has been granted.
predicates.claimant_owned_occupied_land: The claimant had title to the land that another person occupied.
predicates.known_trespass: The claimant knew that another person had entered onto the land.
predicates.no_prompt_objection: The claimant did not promptly object or seek relief while the structures were being built.
predicates.longstanding_structures: The structures had remained on the occupied land for many years.

issues.definition: When a claimant owned occupied land, knew of the occupation, failed to object promptly, and permanent structures remained for many years, the occupier may be required to pay the assessed land value instead of surrendering the land and removing the structures.
